cases.structuralDistinction: The solve begins by excluding three suspects from the victim’s room rather than locating the culprit directly. Two furniture adjacencies and an ordering clue then turn the irregular five-room plan into a constrained room-membership chain.
intendedReasoningPath: Use the three different-room statements to narrow the victim’s possible companion without naming that person directly.
Place Tomas and Ivo from their furniture adjacencies, then use the gallery geometry to restrict their rows and rooms.
Apply the remaining left/edge relationship; the one-per-row and one-per-column rule fixes the last pair and reveals the shared-room suspect.

cases.structuralDistinction: No pairwise ordering clue is provided. The case is driven by two different furniture adjacencies, an interior-only placement, one room exclusion and one positive room assignment across six compact rooms.
intendedReasoningPath: Anchor Nessa beside the tariff shelf and Elias beside the quayside planter; each adjacency still leaves more than one legal square.
Use Jonah’s interior position and Nessa’s room exclusion to remove the tempting mirrored placements.
Place Mirelle in the quay room; row/column uniqueness then forces Arun and Jonah, leaving exactly one suspect in Elias’s room.

cases.structuralDistinction: The clue set avoids direct rows, columns, rooms and furniture. Five above/left relations create a partial-order lattice, while one not-edge fact breaks the last geometric symmetry.
intendedReasoningPath: Build the horizontal chain Cato → Bram → Orin → Neve from the three left-of statements.
Combine Cato-above-Bram and Bram-above-Elara to establish the vertical ordering without assigning exact rows.
Use Elara’s interior-only square with one-per-row/column placement; the irregular rooms then determine which suspect shares Orin’s room.

cases.structuralDistinction: Unlike the relationship-led cases, this board starts with two explicit rows and two explicit columns assigned to different people. The remaining two clues prevent a routine coordinate fill by controlling room and furniture placement.
intendedReasoningPath: Mark Mara’s and Lyra’s rows, then Priya’s and Niko’s columns; do not assume those facts determine complete cells.
Use Priya’s room exclusion and Lyra’s adjacency to the relay desk to select among the coordinate intersections.
The unused row and column force Galen’s position, after which the victim-room rule identifies the responsible suspect.

cases.structuralDistinction: Three people are known only to be somewhere on the perimeter. Positive and negative room evidence must be combined with one vertical relationship, so edge facts act as a coupled constraint rather than isolated placements.
intendedReasoningPath: Separate the three perimeter candidates using Theo’s heated gallery room and Anya’s exclusion from the potting passage.
Place Suri in the seed room; the irregular room boundaries remove edge squares that initially appear interchangeable.
Use Felix-above-Iris and row/column uniqueness to settle the remaining edge cells and expose the shared-room suspect.

cases.structuralDistinction: Each clue uses a different mechanism. The sole same-room clue links two suspects who are not with the victim, forcing the player to distinguish a useful room relationship from the final culprit condition.
intendedReasoningPath: Keep Cass and Dima together while respecting Cass’s row and room exclusion; this pair is deliberately not the victim pair.
Anchor Oren’s column and Vera’s adjacency to the courtyard fern, then apply Vera-left-of-Dima.
Row/column uniqueness leaves June’s room with exactly one remaining suspect; verify that the Cass/Dima pair occupies a different room before accusing.
